narrative:
The model estimates a 66% chance that you will leave your job, which is why your promotion request has been denied. This prediction is driven primarily by three key factors about your profile.

Your relatively short overall work experience of 1-5 years was the strongest factor pushing the model toward predicting you will stay. Most employees the model expects to remain with their employer also fall into this early-career group, so the system sees your limited experience as a stabilizing element rather than a risk.

However, two other aspects pulled more strongly in the opposite direction. The fact that you have received other job offers while working here was the most powerful reason the model leaned toward you eventually leaving. Having external opportunities is a clear signal that you may be considering moves elsewhere. Additionally, working in the “other” sector rather than in medical or education fields also increased the predicted likelihood of departure. Employees in those more structured sectors tend to stay longer, while your sector shows higher turnover in the data the model has learned from.

Taken together, the combination of outside opportunities and your industry outweighed the stabilizing effect of your early-career stage, tipping the prediction above 50%.

The organization should discuss retention strategies with you, especially around career growth and exploring whether internal opportunities can match what external employers are offering. You may also want to reflect on what would make staying feel like the clearer choice.
